extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and parties (patent owners, petitioners, counsel) participating in AIA proceedings before the PTAB (IPR, PGR, CBM, derivation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for petitions, motions, discovery, testimony, protective orders, and institution decisions in AIA trials before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). Intended to govern preparation, filing, and litigation strategy for IPR, PGR, CBM, and derivation proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealing and protective order with petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may, concurrent with filing the petition, file a motion to seal with a proposed protective order; a petitioner filing information under seal with a petition is not required to serve the confidential information. A petitioner may seek entry of the default protective order (Appendix B) or an alternative protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the default protective order is sought, the patent owner may obtain access prior to institution by agreeing to its terms (Board anticipates e-filing confirmation). If an alternative protective order is sought, the patent owner may access sealed information before institution only by: (1) agreeing to petitioner's protective order terms; (2) agreeing to a jointly filed protective order; or (3) obtaining entry of a protective order (e.g., default). Parties may conference with the Board to resolve which protective order should be entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expungement of confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information subject to a protective order ordinarily becomes public 45 days after denial of a petition to institute or 45 days after final judgment in a trial; information referred to in institution or in a final written decision is expected to be made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party seeking to maintain confidentiality may file a motion to expunge before the information becomes public (§ 42.56). The rule balances protecting confidential info and public file history; parties are encouraged to redact sensitive information rather than seal entire documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealing in derivation proceedings (conception dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party in a derivation submitting dates of conception to establish inventorship may file such information under seal and may request that an opponent not be given access to the conception dates until the opponent's conception dates have been provided to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to protect sensitive inventorship evidence while preserving fair adjudication of derivation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery sequenced to narrow scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is sequenced upon institution to develop a fair record and assess credibility, beginning with the patent owner, allowing meaningful discovery before motions and oppositions; discovery is focused on what parties reasonably need to respond to the grounds raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing helps continually narrow the scope of the trial and streamline proceedings (Board sets discovery periods/times in Scheduling Order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine discovery defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery includes: (1) production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony; (2) cross-examination of the other side's declarants; and (3) relevant information that is inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board authorization is not required for routine discovery, but the Board will set the times for conducting it in the Scheduling Order. Routine discovery places parties on a level playing field and streamlines proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of inconsistent statements/work
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosures of inconsistent statements are involved, a party must provide non-privileged work that is inconsistent with contentions relied upon (e.g., non-privileged work undertaken that contradicts an expert affidavit; evidence inconsistent with asserted unexpected results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: petitioner relying on an expert affidavit that a patented method cannot be carried out must provide non-privileged inconsistent work; patent owner relying on unexpected results should provide non-privileged inconsistent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness expenses allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden and expense of producing a witness for redirect or cross-examination should normally fall on the party presenting the witness, including expert fees and travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to witnesses employed by a party, experts, and non-party witnesses. If testimony is presented by transcript, the same cost rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document translation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All proceedings before the Board will be conducted in English; translations must be provided for documents produced in discovery and for all documents relied on or used during the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents in another language without an accompanying English translation will not be considered by the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery: motion and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for additional discovery must be made by motion (parties may agree among themselves), and types of discovery available under the Federal Rules may be sought; the standard for granting such requests varies by proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard is 'interests of justice' for IPR and derivation, and 'good cause' for PGR and CBM. Requests may be granted when evidence uniquely resides with the requesting party or when justice requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled testimony authorization and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A party can request authorization to compel testimony under 35 U.S.C. 24. If granted, testimony may be (1) ex parte, subject to subsequent cross-examination, or (2) inter partes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should discuss appropriate procedure prior to moving. See Appendix D for guidance; consider which form (ex parte vs inter partes) is appropriate given circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 42.51(a) provides for mandatory initial disclosures either by agreement (option 1 or 2) or, if parties fail to agree, by motion if granted; disclosures must be submitted by the time of the patent owner's preliminary response or expiration of that filing period when proceeding under § 42.51(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon institution, parties may automatically take discovery of information identified in initial disclosures; initial disclosures should be filed as exhibits as soon as reasonably practicable to permit related discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures — Option 1 (FRCP-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 1 (modeled after Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A)) requires disclosure of: (1) the name and, if known, contact information of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information (unless solely for impeachment); and (2) a copy or description by category and location of all documents, ESI, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that may be used to support its claims or defenses (unless solely for impeachment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These disclosures permit automatic discovery upon institution and must be filed as exhibits to enable discovery related to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures — Option 2 (expanded disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 2 is more extensive and, if applicable, requires: I) when petitioning based on alleged prior non‑published public disclosure, identification of persons likely to know of the prior disclosure, contacts, representation status, documents relating to the disclosure, and physical items (descriptions, locations, and whether they will be produced); and II) when petitioning on obviousness grounds, analogous identification of persons and items relating to secondary indicia of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes detailed lists of witnesses, documents, photographs, analyses, computer code, and production plans for inspection/analysis/testing/sampling; this enables targeted discovery upon institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live testimony when demeanor critical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may require live testimony where the demeanor of a witness is critical to assessing credibility (e.g., derivation issues, alleged misconduct, interpreter use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examination may be ordered to take place before an administrative patent judge, at the deposition or at oral argument. See Appendix D for testimony guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default time limits for witness examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 42.53(c)(1) and (c)(2), default time limits are: compelled testimony — seven hours direct, four hours cross, two hours redirect; uncompelled direct testimony — seven hours cross, four hours redirect, two hours recross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony may be taken at any reasonable location in the United States; parties should agree on location or use Board assistance (conference call) to resolve disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-discovery default model order
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to e-discovery costs, the Office adopts a default Model Order Regarding E-Discovery (Appendix C) based on the Federal Circuit's Model Order and modified for statutory differences; Rule 502 of the Federal Rules of Evidence is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The default Model Order will be entered in a proceeding whenever ESI discovery is sought (except routine discovery). Parties desiring ESI production should raise the matter with the Board in a timely fashion before discovery is scheduled.

rubrics_metrics.name: General motions practice and prior authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings begin with a petition; additional relief must be requested by motion (§ 42.20(a)). Generally, motions require prior Board authorization (§ 42.20(b)), except where impractical or where authorization is automatically granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions where impractical include motions to seal and motions filed with a petition (e.g., motions to waive page limits). Motions automatically authorized (without a conference) include requests for rehearing, observations on cross-examination, and motions to exclude evidence. Initial conference calls typically serve to obtain authorization and resolve procedural issues quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page limits for filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Page limits apply to petitions, motions, patent owner preliminary responses/responses, oppositions, and replies: 60 pages for IPR petitions and derivation proceedings; 80 pages for PGR and CBM petitions; 15 pages for motions. Patent owner prelim/responses limited to equal number of pages as corresponding petition; oppositions equal to corresponding motion; replies to patent owner responses limited to 15 pages; replies to oppositions limited to 5 pages (§ 42.24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: concise, well‑organized writing is encouraged. Parties are not required to submit statements of material fact (§ 42.22). Claim charts need not be double‑spaced (§ 42.6(a)(2)(iii)); claim charts count toward page limits when part of the filing, but exhibits from other proceedings submitted as exhibits do not count toward page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony must disclose underlying facts/data
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits expressing an expert opinion must disclose the underlying facts or data upon which the opinion is based (see Fed. R. Evid. 705 and § 42.65).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions lacking disclosure of underlying facts/data may be given little or no weight; unsupported assertions are not to be credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and data — provide explanatory information
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties relying on scientific tests and data (e.g., spectroscopy graphs, HPLC data) should provide, in addition to § 42.65 explanations, any other information believed to assist the Board in understanding the significance of the test or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context, methodology, and relevant supporting information so the Board can assess the probative value of test results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, the Board will review objective evidence (secondary considerations) of nonobviousness proffered by the patent owner when determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners should present such evidence where relevant; initial disclosures (Option 2) may require identification of persons and documents relating to secondary indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum procedural compliance for petition filing
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a filing date a petition must meet minimum statutory standards (e.g., § 42.106; 35 U.S.C. 312(a)) — a complete petition must be filed with the required fee and include a certificate of service for the petition, fee, and evidence relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IPR, the petitioner must certify the patent is eligible for IPR and that the petitioner is not barred/estopped, identify challenged claims, and state the specific basis for the challenge (§ 42.104). Similar petition requirements exist for PGR (§ 42.204), CBM (§ 42.304), and derivation (§ 42.404).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for institution threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in a proceeding before the Board is a preponderance of the evidence standard (§ 42.1(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard governs the Board's evaluation of merits-related evidence at the institution stage and beyond, subject to the statutory institution thresholds discussed separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific petition content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must certify availability for review and that it is not barred/estopped; identify each challenged claim and the specific statutory grounds for each challenge; provide a claim construction for challenged claims; and state the relevance of evidence to issues raised. For IPR, PGR, and CBM, a petitioner must identify how the construed claim is unpatentable over the relevant evidence (§§ 42.104(b), 42.204(b), 42.304(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must present claim-by-claim grounds and supporting evidence sufficient to meet the applicable statutory institution threshold for the proceeding sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered business method (CBM) demonstration and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A CBM petitioner must demonstrate the patent is a covered business method patent (§ 42.304(a)); covered business method patents claim methods or apparatus for data processing or operations used in practice/administration/management of financial product/service, excluding technological inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of techniques that typically do not render a patent a technological invention: mere recitation of known technologies (hardware/network/software), reciting use of known prior art technology to accomplish a process, or combining prior art structures to achieve predictable results. Example CBM patents: methods for hedging risk in commodities trading; methods for verifying credit card transactions. Example non-CBM (technological) patents: novel hedging machine; novel credit card reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim charts usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts are optional but may help explain how a claim maps to a reference, specification, or another claim; they can streamline identification of key claim features and comparison to evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim charts submitted as part of a petition/motion/prelim response/response/opposition/reply count toward applicable page limits; claim charts need not be double-spaced to reduce page count. Claim charts from other proceedings submitted as exhibits do not count toward page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (broadest reasonable interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) standard to construe challenged, amended, or new claims during IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings (consistent with §§ 42.100(b), 42.200(b), 42.300(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may simply state that claim terms are given their BRI as understood by one of ordinary skill consistent with the disclosure, or propose a specific construction supported by disclosure citations. BRI encourages clear, unambiguous claim drafting and is consistent across Office proceedings; patent owners may file motions to amend (first motion after conferring with Board; additional motions with good cause or joint request to materially advance settlement) (§§ 42.121, 42.221).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner preliminary response timing and content
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPR, PGR, and CBM proceedings, a patent owner may file a preliminary response no later than three months after the grant of a filing date (§§ 42.107(b), 42.207(b)). The preliminary response may present evidence other than new testimonial evidence to demonstrate that no review should be instituted; new testimonial evidence may be permitted where in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential arguments include: petitioner is statutorily barred; asserted references are not prior art; prior art lacks material limitation in all independent claims; prior art teaches away; petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable; for 101 grounds in PGR, provide brief explanation of patent eligibility. Patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response to expedite proceeding without adverse inference; statutory disclaimer of challenged claims may terminate or narrow proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory institution thresholds by proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Different statutory thresholds apply for institution: (a) IPR — Director may not institute unless petition and any response show a reasonable likelihood the petitioner would prevail on at least one challenged claim (35 U.S.C. 314(a)); (b) PGR — Director may not institute unless petition (if unrebutted) would demonstrate it is more likely than not (>50%) that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (35 U.S.C. 324(a)); PGR may also be satisfied by a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents (35 U.S.C. 324(b)); (c) CBM — transitional CBM treated as PGR with additional standing requirement (suit/charge of infringement) and exclusion for technological inventions; (d) Derivation — petition must state with particularity basis for derivation, be filed within one year of first publication of the earlier applicant's claim, be made under oath, and be supported by substantial evidence (35 U.S.C. 135(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards vary in stringency (PGR >50% vs IPR reasonable likelihood). CBM has statutory standing limitation. Derivation requires particularized and timely factual showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations in instituting a review (325(d), timeliness, complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding institution, the Board considers whether the petitioner satisfied the statutory standard and may take into account whether the same or substantially the same prior art/arguments were previously presented to the Office under 35 U.S.C. 325(d). The Board may decline to institute where it could not complete the proceeding timely or where complexity (many claims/references or need for extensive foreign witness testimony) would prevent timely completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board exercises discretion to manage docket and ensure trials can be completed within statutory timeframes; petitions seeking overly broad or unmanageable reviews may be denied on administrative grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and scope of institution decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board institutes a trial, it will streamline issues by authorizing trial only on challenged claims and grounds that meet threshold standards, identifying grounds on a claim-by-claim basis; any claim/issue not included is not part of the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no trial is instituted, the decision will typically contain a short statement why standards were not met. The Board's determination whether to institute is final and nonappealable (35 U.S.C. 314(d), 325(d), 324(e); § 42.71(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling Order requirements and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will provide a Scheduling Order (Appendix A) concurrent with the decision to institute, setting due dates for actions to ensure trial completion within one year of institution; parties may request changes to due dates at the initial conference call and stipulate different dates for Due Dates 1 through 5 (but not later than Due Date 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling Order accounts for proceeding complexity but enforces the one-year completion target; parties should raise scheduling preferences early (initial conference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial conference call procedure and motions list
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board expects to hold an initial conference call within about one month of institution to discuss the Scheduling Order and anticipated motions. Parties should provide a list of proposed motions no later than two business days prior to the call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accurate motions list helps the Board and opposing parties prepare, permits the Board to adjust schedule, determines necessary/sufficient motions, and may reveal dispositive issues. Submission of the list does not preclude later additional motions, though prior authorization may be required and set times may remain unchanged.
